record.paper_title: On some open problems related to the restricted Burnside problem.
record.original_question: Let G be an m-generated linear group with a chosen generating m-tuple, and let F_m be the free group on m generators. If there exists a polynomial that annihilates every value obtained by evaluating a primitive word of F_m on the chosen generators of G, must G be soluble-by-finite?

evidence.quote: Another problem asks whether an m-generated linear group is soluble-by-finite if there is a polynomial that annihilates all values of primitive words on the generators.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $m\ge 1$ be an integer and let $F_m$ denote the free group on $m$ generators $x_1,\dots,x_m$. A word $w\in F_m$ is called primitive if it belongs to some free generating set of $F_m$. Let $G\le \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ be an $m$-generated linear group over a field $K$, with a fixed generating $m$-tuple $(g_1,\dots,g_m)\in G^m$. For each primitive word $w\in F_m$, let $w(g_1,\dots,g_m)\in G\subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ denote its evaluation.

Suppose there exists a nonzero polynomial $p(t)\in K[t]$ such that $p(w(g_1,\dots,g_m))=0$ in the matrix algebra $M_n(K)$ for every primitive word $w\in F_m$. Must $G$ be soluble-by-finite (i.e., contain a soluble subgroup of finite index)?
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface a published resolution of this specific question about m-generated linear groups in which a single polynomial annihilates the evaluations of all primitive words of F_m. No source confirming a proof or counterexample was found, so the current status appears to be unknown/open based on available evidence.
